# The question {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

## Do bigger houses really sell for more — and by *how much*?

A dataset of house sales: for each house we see **two** numbers — its **size** and its **price**.

. . .

Eyeballing one house tells us nothing. The *relationship between the two columns* is the story — and
we want to **measure** it, not just sense it.

::: {.notes}
Open with the concrete question. We have bivariate data: two measurements per observation. The whole
chapter is about summarizing the link between them with a number and a line.
:::

## Where we're going

::: {.incremental}
- **See** the relationship — scatterplots and two-way tables
- **Measure** its strength — correlation and covariance
- **Model** it — the ordinary-least-squares (OLS) regression line
- **Judge** the fit — $R^2$ and the standard error of the regression
- **Interpret** it honestly — association is not causation
:::

## Three ideas carry the whole chapter

**Association** — do $x$ and $y$ tend to move together, and in which direction?

**Correlation** $r$ — a single, unit-free number in $[-1, 1]$ for the *strength* of a **linear** link.

**Regression** — a line $\hat{y} = b_1 + b_2 x$ that *predicts* $y$ from $x$.

[Summarizing a relationship means turning a cloud of points into a direction, a number, and a line.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These three terms recur in every later chapter. Correlation measures; regression predicts.
:::

# Seeing and measuring the link {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Act II · The investigation]{.act}

## Start by looking: price rises with size — but not perfectly

![Each dot is a house. The upward drift is the association; the scatter around it is everything size *doesn't* explain.](figures/fig_5-3_01.png)

[A scatterplot is the first summary of bivariate data — direction and spread, before any number.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Point out the clear positive slope and the vertical spread at any given size — other factors (lot,
age, location) move price too.
:::

## Draw the scatterplot in a few lines

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7|8-9|10"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt               # plotting

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
houses = pd.read_stata(url)                  # load the 29 Davis, CA house sales

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))      # create one figure + axes
ax.scatter(houses["size"], houses["price"],  # x = size, y = price
           s=80, alpha=0.7, color="#22d3ee") # marker size, transparency, colour
plt.show()                                   # render the scatter plot
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
matplotlib is the workhorse plotting library. One `scatter` call turns the two columns into the
picture on the previous slide.
:::

## Correlation measures strength; covariance only gives the sign

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Covariance
- sign tells the **direction**
- carries the **units** of $x \times y$ (dollars × sq ft)
- scale is not comparable across datasets
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Correlation $r$
- **unit-free**, always in $[-1, 1]$
- $r = s_{xy} / (s_x s_y)$
- comparable across any pair of variables
:::
::::

[Covariance says *which way*; correlation says *how strongly* — on a scale anyone can read.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## $r$ captures *linear* strength — and can miss a curve

![Same idea, four strengths: strong, moderate, none, and negative. Correlation ranks the first three by how tightly points hug a line.](figures/fig_x_01.png)

[$r$ near $\pm 1$ means a tight line; $r \approx 0$ means no *linear* link — not necessarily no link at all.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Zero correlation can still hide a strong non-linear relationship (e.g. a U-shape). r only sees the
straight-line part. For our house data r = 0.7858.
:::

## Measure the link: correlation and covariance in pandas

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7|9-10"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
houses = pd.read_stata(url)                  # load the 29 Davis, CA house sales

cov = houses[["price", "size"]].cov()        # covariance matrix (carries units: $ × sq ft)
corr = houses[["price", "size"]].corr()      # correlation matrix (unit-free, in −1…1)

r = corr.loc["price", "size"]                # pull out the single correlation number
print(f"r = {r:.4f}")                        # → r = 0.7858
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
`.corr()` and `.cov()` are pandas DataFrame methods. The off-diagonal cell is the number we want;
correlation standardizes covariance by the two standard deviations.
:::

## The regression line turns the cloud into a prediction

$$\hat{y} = b_1 + b_2\, x$$

[$b_1$ is the **intercept** (predicted $y$ when $x = 0$); $b_2$ is the **slope** — the predicted change
in $y$ for a one-unit increase in $x$. OLS picks $b_1, b_2$ to minimize the sum of squared residuals.]{.comment}

::: {.notes}
Define residual e_i = y_i − ŷ_i. OLS minimizes Σ e_i². This generalizes the sample mean: an
intercept-only regression returns ȳ.
:::

## OLS draws the single best-fitting line through the cloud

![The fitted line: ŷ = 115,017 + 73.77 × size. Each extra square foot predicts about \$74 more.](figures/fig_x_02.png)

[Slope $b_2 = \$73.77$ per sq ft; intercept $b_1 = \$115{,}017$ — a house 100 sq ft larger is predicted to cost about **\$7,377** more.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The slope is the economically meaningful number. The intercept here is an out-of-range
extrapolation (no 0-sq-ft houses), so don't over-interpret it.
:::

## Fit the regression line in Python

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-8|10-11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                   # install pyfixest in Colab (-q = quiet; not preinstalled)

import pandas as pd                         # pandas → load & handle tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                        # pyfixest → fast OLS regression + tidy output

# dataset: 29 house sales in Davis, CA (price, size, bedrooms, …)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
houses = pd.read_stata(url)                 # read the Stata .dta file into a DataFrame

m = pf.feols("price ~ size", data=houses)   # fit OLS: regress price on size
m.summary()                                 # report intercept b1, slope b2, SEs, R²
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained — paste it into an empty Colab cell and it runs end to end: load the AED house
data straight from the project's open-data repo, then fit and report the regression. pyfixest is
the project's estimation package. (The deck itself doesn't execute; this is the runnable workflow.)
:::

## $R^2$ splits total variation into explained and left-over

$$R^2 = \frac{\text{explained SS}}{\text{total SS}} = 1 - \frac{\text{residual SS}}{\text{total SS}}$$

![Total variation in price = what the line explains + what it leaves in the residuals.](figures/fig_x_03.png)

[Here $R^2 = 0.617$: size explains about **62%** of the variation in price, leaving 38% to everything else. (And $R^2 = r^2 = 0.7858^2$.)]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
For simple regression R² always equals r². The standard error of the regression, s_e, measures the
typical residual in the units of y (dollars).
:::

## A flexible curve checks the straight-line assumption

![Nonparametric regression lets the data choose the shape — if it tracks the OLS line, linearity is a fair summary.](figures/fig_5-11_01.png)

[Fit a flexible curve first; if it hugs the straight line, the simple linear summary is trustworthy.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Nonparametric regression imposes no functional form. Comparing it to the OLS line is a quick,
honest check that the linear model isn't hiding curvature.
:::

# Reading it right {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

## The tempting mistake — and the correction

[Objection.]{.objection} "Size and price have $r = 0.79$, so **larger size causes higher price**."

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} **Association is not causation.** Confounders (location; lot size, though only weakly linked to size and price here), reverse
causality, and selection can all create a correlation. A line summarizes; it does not identify a cause.

[A correlation earns a causal reading only with a design that rules out the alternatives.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- A **scatterplot** is the first, honest summary of two variables.
- **Correlation** $r \in [-1, 1]$ measures *linear* strength, unit-free; **covariance** gives only the sign.
- **OLS** fits $\hat{y} = b_1 + b_2 x$ by minimizing squared residuals; the **slope** is the headline.
- **$R^2$** reports the share of variation explained — and $R^2 = r^2$ for simple regression.
- **Association $\neq$ causation** — always the last word on interpretation.
:::

# Measure the relationship, model it with a line — then resist calling it a cause. {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}
